title: Low mood after having a baby

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi Chloe, come in. And this must be Oscar? And you're...?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Jamie. Chloe's partner.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Lovely to meet you. Chloe, is it okay for Jamie to be here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I want him here.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How old is Oscar now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Eight weeks. No, ten. He's ten weeks on Saturday. I've lost track of time.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's very normal. What's been happening?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just don't feel like myself. I cry all the time. I don't enjoy anything, not even him. And I feel so guilty saying that.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for telling me. How long have you felt like this?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About six weeks. It started a few weeks after he was born and it hasn't lifted.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How are you sleeping, when Oscar lets you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Even when he's asleep, I can't sleep. I just lie there worrying.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What do you worry about?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Everything. That something will happen to him. I get these horrible pictures in my head, like what if I drop him down the stairs. I'd never do anything to him. I hate the thoughts. I won't carry him on the stairs now.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for telling me. Thoughts like that are really common in new mums, especially when you're anxious, and they're upsetting precisely because you don't want them. Have you ever had any urge or intention to harm Oscar?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Never. I love him.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And have you had any thoughts about harming yourself, or that you'd be better off not here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sometimes I think they'd be better off without me. But I wouldn't do anything. I've got Oscar.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you made any plans?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you had depression before?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When I was 19. I was on fluoxetine for a year and it helped.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Does anyone in your family have mental health problems?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My mum had to go into hospital after she had my brother. She was really unwell, hearing things. They never really talked about it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's important, thank you. Are you breastfeeding?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any medicines or allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Can I just say, I've been struggling too. I've had a couple of panic attacks at work.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you, Jamie. It's important you get support too. Please book to see your own GP.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I will.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Chloe, your PHQ-9 score today is 17, which fits with moderately severe depression. This is postnatal depression, and it's treatable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to start a medicine called sertraline, 50 milligrams once a day. It's one of the safest antidepressants when breastfeeding.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Because of how you're feeling, and your mum's history, I'm going to refer you to the perinatal mental health team. I'll also let your health visitor know.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And I'll give you the details for Talking Therapies. They prioritise new parents.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to see you again in one week.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If the thoughts about not being here get stronger, or you feel you can't keep yourself safe, call 111 and choose the mental health option, or call 999. And if you ever feel confused or start seeing or hearing things that aren't there, get help urgently.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll make sure she does.

reference_note.history: Low mood for 6 weeks, starting a few weeks after delivery: tearful, anhedonia, guilt. Poor sleep even when the baby sleeps; persistent worry. Intrusive, unwanted thoughts of accidentally dropping the baby, which distress her; no urge or intent to harm the baby; avoids carrying him on the stairs. Passive thoughts that her family would be better off without her; no plans or intent; protective factor: baby. Previous depression at 19, treated with fluoxetine for a year. Her mother was admitted to hospital with a severe mental illness after a birth (possible postpartum psychosis). Breastfeeding. Partner has had panic attacks recently; advised to see his own GP.
reference_note.medications_allergies: No regular medications. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.impression: Moderately severe postnatal depression with intrusive harm-related thoughts (ego-dystonic) and passive suicidal ideation without plan. Family history of possible postpartum psychosis.
reference_note.plan: Start sertraline 50 mg once daily (compatible with breastfeeding). Refer to the perinatal mental health team. Inform health visitor. Talking Therapies details given (priority for new parents). Review in 1 week.
reference_note.safety_netting: If suicidal thoughts worsen or unable to keep herself safe, call NHS 111 (mental health option) or 999. Seek urgent help if confusion or hallucinations.
